## The one sentence to leave with

> **A function is handed a copy — unless it is handed an address, and an array is neither.**

That single distinction decides every problem today. It is why `swap` needs `&a` and
`countNeighbours(world, i, j)` does not; why `minMax` cannot simply `return` its answer;
and why a function you hand a grid to can quietly change it underneath you.

## The three drills that carry the week

Do `d02`, `d03` and `d06` **in that order**, and predict each before you press Enter.
They are one argument in three steps:

| | what it does | what it shows |
|---|---|---|
| `d02` | `addOne(x)` — and `x` is still 5 | a **copy** went in |
| `d03` | one character different: `reallyAddOne(&x)` — `x` is 6 | an **address** went in |
| `d06` | `wipe(a)` — no `&` anywhere, and yet `a[0]` changed | an array is **already** an address |

If `d06` surprises you, good — that is the point of it, and it is the licence for every
`nextGeneration(world)` call in the second half of the afternoon.

## Act 1 · Drills — predict, then run (20 min, not marked)

```bash
./drill.sh --all
```

Ten small programs. Each one is shown to you, you type what you think it will print, and
only then does it run. **Predicting is the exercise.**

| Drills | Territory |
|---|---|
| `d01`–`d04` | what a function hands back, and what it cannot change — `d02` and `d03` differ by **one character** and give different answers |
| `d05`–`d06` | the swap that does nothing, and the array that changes anyway **without any `&`** |
| `d07`–`d08` | a grid subscript, and a counter that lives in the caller |
| `d09`–`d10` | a corner cell's neighbours, and `return` from inside a loop |

::: {.callout-warning}
**`d05`, `d06` and `d09` are each a graded problem in miniature.** `d05` is `b2` before you
fix it. `d06` is the licence for every `nextGeneration(world)` you will write — an array
needs no `&`, and changes anyway. `d09` is `e3`, ten marks, already written for you at one
corner. Predict all three on paper before you run them.
:::

These carry **no marks at all**. A wrong prediction costs you nothing — which is exactly
why you should write it down before pressing Enter.

## Working on one problem — read this once

The same four steps for all ten. Take `b1_sumto.c`:

```bash
vim b1_sumto.c          # or nano, or gedit — whatever you use
gcc b1_sumto.c -o b1    # compile it, naming the program b1
./b1                    # run it, and type the input it asks for
./check.sh b1           # only when it runs: mark it
```

Running it yourself looks like this — you type the `5`:

```
$ ./b1
Enter n: 5
total=15
```

**No `-lm`, no extra flags.** Every problem this week compiles with plain `gcc`, and none of
them may use `math.h`. If you reach for `sqrt` or `cos` from the library, you have skipped
the exercise.

::: {.callout-tip}
Compile and run it *yourself* before you run `./check.sh`. The checker tells you whether the
answer is right; running it tells you what your program actually does. You need both, and the
second one is faster.
:::

**The world problems take 64 numbers**, which nobody wants to type. Two sample worlds are
already in your workspace, so feed them in from a file with `<`:

```bash
./e4 < blinker.txt
```

```
........
........
...#....
...#....
...#....
........
........
........
```

`e3` and `e5` want an extra number *after* the 64 — the cell for `e3`, the generation count
for `e5`. Add it on the end:

```bash
(cat blinker.txt; echo "3 3") | ./e3     # -> neighbours=2
(cat glider.txt;  echo 4)     | ./e5     # -> alive=5
```

Make your own worlds too: copy `blinker.txt`, edit the 0s and 1s, and watch what happens.

::: {.callout-warning}
The starters **do not compile as shipped**. Each blank is a name the compiler has never heard
of, so `gcc` points at the exact line still waiting for you — something like

```
b1_sumto.c:13:5: error: 'TODO_body' undeclared
```

The wording differs between compilers; the part that matters is the **file and line number**,
which is the blank you have not filled yet. That is the intended first error, not a broken
file.
:::

## Act 2 · Fill the blanks (25 min · 5 marks each)

In all five, **the function's first line is already written** and `main` is already calling
it exactly as written. That line is the *promise* — what goes in, what comes back. Keep it;
do not change it.

| File | What it does | Final line ends with exactly |
|---|---|---|
| `b1_sumto.c` | `1 + 2 + … + n`, now inside a function that must `return` | `total=<S>` |
| `b2_swap.c` | exchange the caller's two integers — drill `d05`, made to work | `a=<B> b=<A>` |
| `b3_minmax.c` | smallest **and** largest of `n` values — two answers, neither returned | `lo=<L> hi=<H>` |
| `b4_rowsum.c` | the total of row `r` of a 4 × 4 grid | `sum=<S>` |
| `b5_cos.c` | cos *x* from the **first `n` terms** of its series | `cos=<V>`, `%.6f` |

The signature is given in each file — `int sumTo(int n)`, `void swap(int *a, int *b)`,
`void minMax(int a[], int n, int *lo, int *hi)`, `int rowSum(int m[][COLS], int r)`,
`double cosSeries(double x, int n)`. Read the `GIVEN` comment at the top of each starter for
the exact input range.

::: {.callout-tip}
`b4` is worth pausing on. The row count may be left out of that parameter; the **column
count may not**. Reaching `m[r][j]` means computing `r*COLS + j`, and without `COLS` there
is no sum to do.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
`b5` has a trap with a body count. Do **not** compute each term's factorial with its own
inner loop — 13! already overflows an `int` and the answer goes quietly, plausibly wrong.
Build each term from the one before it:

```c
term = term * (-x*x) / ((2*k+1) * (2*k+2));
```

starting at `term = 1.0`. No factorial is ever formed, and nothing overflows.
:::

## Act 3 · The checked five (55 min, solo · 10 marks each)

These give you the specification and nothing else.

| Problem | Task | Final line ends with exactly |
|---|---|---|
| `e1.c` | the *x* ≥ 0 with **x³ + x = a**, by halving | `root=<R>`, `%.4f` |
| `e2.c` | a 4 × 4 grid flipped about its diagonal | *(the whole output is compared)* |
| `e3.c` | how many of the **eight** cells touching (r, c) are alive | `neighbours=<N>` |
| `e4.c` | **one generation** of the Game of Life | *(the whole grid is compared)* |
| `e5.c` | how many cells are alive after `g` generations | `alive=<N>` |

`e1` — there is no formula to rearrange. Halve the interval, as Monday did, and write it as
**two** functions: one for the left-hand side, one that does the halving and calls it. The
answer is somewhere in [0, a].

`e2` — build the answer in a **second** grid. Writing the flip back into the original
overwrites values you have not read yet, which is `e4`'s trap met early on something small.

`e3` — two things can go wrong and only one is obvious. Skipping the cell itself is the
obvious one. The other is the edge: a corner cell **has** only three neighbours, and reaching
for the other five reads outside the array. C will not stop you, and it will often appear to
work.

`e4` — **this is the problem the whole lab has been pointing at.** See the warning below.

`e5` — watch `g = 0`. A loop written "do it, then check" runs once even when it was asked for
none. And if you find yourself re-writing the rule, stop: `e4` already contains it.

::: {.callout-note}
`e3`, `e4` and `e5` are deliberately **one program grown three times**. Write
`countNeighbours` once for `e3` and copy it into `e4`; put the generation in a *function*
in `e4` and `e5` costs you three more lines. If you find yourself copying the whole rule
into a fresh loop for `e5`, stop — that is the moment a function was supposed to save you.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**The one that decides `e4`.** Every cell in a generation must see the *same old world*.
Decide the whole next generation into a second grid, then copy it back. If you write each
cell's answer straight into `world`, cell (0,1) counts a neighbour that has already
changed — and the blinker below will visibly fall apart instead of flipping.
:::

Two sample worlds ship in your workspace so you can watch it run rather than trust it:

```bash
./e4 < blinker.txt      # three in a row should become three in a column
./e4 < glider.txt       # a shape that walks
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Tuesday's lecture printed a live cell as `##` and a dead one as two blanks, which reads
well on a projector. Here it is **`#` and `.`** — a checker cannot see blank space.
:::

**How checking works** — `./check.sh e3` compiles *your source* and runs it on the public
examples printed in your starter **and on fresh random inputs drawn from the GIVEN**. A
program that memorises an example fails the next draw.

::: {.callout-note}
`e2` and `e4` are compared over the **whole output**, not just the last line, because the
answer is a shape. Spacing is ignored; a missing or wrong row is not. If yours looks right
but fails, run `./check.sh e4` and read the difference it prints rather than squinting at
the screen.
:::

```bash
./check.sh          # everything
./check.sh e4       # just one problem, while you are working on it
```

It prints **your marks, problem by problem**:

```
  YOUR MARKS SO FAR   (blanks 5 each, checked 10 each)

    b1  6/6 vectors    5 of  5 marks
    b2  6/6 vectors    5 of  5 marks
    b3  7/7 vectors    5 of  5 marks
    b4  6/6 vectors    5 of  5 marks
    b5  10/10 vectors    5 of  5 marks
    e1  9/9 vectors   10 of 10 marks
    e2  5/5 vectors   10 of 10 marks
    e3  9/9 vectors   10 of 10 marks
    e4  2/7 vectors    3 of 10 marks
    e5  0/9 vectors    0 of 10 marks
    ---------------------------------------------

```

That `e4` line is the in-place bug: two vectors pass, five do not. Marks are **partial** —
every vector you pass earns its share, so fixing one failing case is always worth doing,
right up to the last minute. Treat the total as an estimate: the random vectors are drawn
fresh on every run, so it can move a mark or two.

Fix, re-check, repeat. Then — green or time-up:

```bash
./check.sh --bundle
```

The bundle lands one directory **above** your workspace, named

machine forgets; you must not.
:::

## Stretch (fast finishers, not marked)

1. **Watch the glider hit the wall.** Our world has hard edges, so the glider cannot walk
   forever. Run it well past `e5`'s twelve generations and print the population each time.
   It does **not** die: at generation 24 it stops changing altogether, leaving four cells
   in the bottom-right corner. Find out what they are.
2. **Find a still life.** That corner leftover is one — a 2×2 block, which has exactly the
   neighbour counts it needs to keep itself alive. Add a check to `e5` that reports the
   first generation identical to the one before it, and confirm it says 24.
3. **Make the world wrap**, so column 7's right-hand neighbour is column 0 and the glider
   never reaches a wall at all. One change, in `countNeighbours` only — and the bounds test
   you fought with in `e3` becomes an arithmetic one instead.

## Reflect

Two questions to be able to answer out loud before you leave — they are what the viva asks:

1. Why does `swap` need `&a` when `countNeighbours(world, i, j)` does not?
2. What exactly breaks if you delete the second grid in `e4` — which cell notices first?
